summary: Former actress from the Hippodrome world of Constantinople who married Justinian I and became empress in 527; she held the court together in the Nika riots of 532, protected the Miaphysite clergy and is portrayed in the San Vitale mosaic at Ravenna.
overview: Theodora rose from a family of Hippodrome performers to become the wife and closest political partner of Justinian I. She is remembered for the speech Procopius gives her in the Nika riots, her protection of the Miaphysite church and the mosaic at Ravenna, while Procopius's Secret History made her the most slandered empress in Byzantine history.
greatestFeats: Persuaded Justinian I and his council not to flee during the Nika riots of 532, according to Procopius
Sheltered Miaphysite bishops and monks in the Hormisdas Palace against her husband's church policy
Founded the Metanoia convent for women leaving prostitution
Named with Justinian in the oath of office sworn by provincial governors from 535
keyAchievements: Portrayed in the San Vitale mosaic at Ravenna

birth.note: The year is not recorded and modern estimates range from about 490 to 500; later Syriac writers placed her birth in Syria.

death.circumstance: Died after an illness that Victor of Tunnuna calls cancer, a word then used for any malignant ulcer or tumour.

quickFacts.knownFor: The Nika riots, her Miaphysite patronage and the Ravenna mosaic

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Theodora was empress of the Eastern Roman Empire from 527 until her death in 548 as the wife of Justinian I. The daughter of a bear keeper at the Hippodrome of Constantinople, she worked on the stage until Justin I changed the law so that his nephew and heir could marry her.

She is remembered for the speech with which, according to Procopius, she stopped the court fleeing during the Nika riots of 532, for protecting the Miaphysite clergy, and for the mosaic in San Vitale at Ravenna that still shows her in full imperial dress. Procopius's Secret History, written after her death, turned her into a byword for vice, and separating the empress from that pamphlet is the central problem in writing about her.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Theodora was probably born in Constantinople around 495. Her father, Acacius, kept the bears of the Green circus faction; after his death the Greens refused to help his widow and daughters, and the rival Blues gave the family work. Theodora followed her elder sister Comito onto the stage, a profession that law and common opinion placed close to prostitution. She became the companion of Hecebolus, governor of the Libyan Pentapolis, was abandoned by him, and returned to the capital by way of Alexandria and Antioch. By the early 520s she had met Justinian, and she already had a daughter, whom she later acknowledged openly.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Almost every portrait of Theodora comes from Procopius, and he painted three. In the Wars she has the courage that saves the throne in 532; in the Buildings, a panegyric for Justinian, she is pious and beautiful; in the Secret History, first printed in 1623, she is a shameless performer turned vindictive tyrant with secret prisons in the palace. The obscene stories of her youth in that book follow a formula in which a good empress is chaste and a bad one lustful and greedy, and David Potter has called them an exaggerated diatribe. Yet Anthony Kaldellis and Clive Foss point out that independent sources confirm the book's outline: her theatrical past, the marriage law and her ruthlessness towards enemies.

Other witnesses show a hard political operator with real commitments. John of Ephesus, a Miaphysite bishop who knew her, praised her charity and her protection of his church while freely admitting that she had come from the brothel. A letter of the Ostrogothic king Theodahad has been read as evidence of her hand in the death of Queen Amalasuntha. She did not forgive opponents: the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian, who had spoken against her to Justinian, was trapped into apparent treason by her and by Antonina, the wife of Belisarius, and exiled in 541.

contentSections.title: Marriage to Justinian
paragraphs: Justinian, nephew and chosen heir of Justin I, could not legally marry her: a law dating back to Constantine barred men of senatorial rank from marrying actresses, and Justin's wife, Euphemia, opposed the match. After Euphemia died in 524, Justin allowed actresses who had left the stage to marry men of any rank. Justinian and Theodora married soon afterwards, probably in 525. When Justin made Justinian co-emperor in April 527, Theodora was crowned augusta, and on Justin's death that August the couple ruled together.

Justinian treated her as a colleague. In his law of 535 against the sale of provincial governorships he called her his partner in deliberation, and officials had to swear loyalty to emperor and empress together. She also arranged marriages that tied her family to the old aristocracy: her sister Comito married the general Sittas, and her niece, the future Empress Sophia, married Justinian's nephew Justin II.

contentSections.title: The Nika riots
paragraphs: In January 532 the Blue and Green factions, furious that the government would not pardon two of their men who had survived a botched hanging, joined forces under the cry “Nika”, meaning “conquer”. They burned much of the centre of Constantinople, including the church of Hagia Sophia, and proclaimed Hypatius, a nephew of the late emperor Anastasius I, as emperor. As Justinian's council discussed escape by sea, Procopius has Theodora declare that for one who has reigned it is intolerable to become a fugitive, and that royal purple makes the finest burial shroud.

The speech is Procopius's composition, and its closing line adapts advice once given to the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse, but it probably reflects a real argument in the palace. The court stayed. The generals Belisarius and Mundus trapped the crowd in the Hippodrome and killed some 30,000 people, and Hypatius and his brother Pompeius were executed, in one account at Theodora's insistence.

contentSections.title: Religion, patronage and power
paragraphs: Theodora openly favoured the Miaphysites, who rejected the Council of Chalcedon, while Justinian tried to bring them back into the imperial church. Procopius and Evagrius suspected the couple of dividing the parties between them on purpose, but her commitment was real. She hid the deposed patriarch Anthimus in her own apartments for years and filled the Hormisdas Palace with Miaphysite monks, so many that a floor is said to have given way beneath them. She helped install Theodosius as patriarch of Alexandria. Pope Silverius, who refused to restore Anthimus, was deposed on her instructions and died in exile on an island.

She also used her position on behalf of women. Early in the reign she and Justinian closed brothels in the capital and bought out the girls held in them, and she founded the Metanoia, or Repentance, a convent on the Asian shore for women leaving prostitution; Procopius sneered that some inmates jumped from its walls to escape. Her name stands beside Justinian's in the dedication inscription of the church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus in Constantinople.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Theodora died in Constantinople on 28 June 548, probably in her early fifties. Victor of Tunnuna says she died of cancer, a term that then covered any malignant ulcer or tumour. She was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles. In 559 Justinian stopped at her tomb to light candles in her memory, and Miaphysite writers say he kept his promise to protect the refugees she had sheltered in the Hormisdas Palace.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Theodora's niece Sophia became empress in 565 as the wife of Justin II, and descendants of her acknowledged daughter married into the family of the emperor Maurice. Her support helped Jacob Baradaeus, whose ordinations created a separate Miaphysite hierarchy in Syria. She is venerated as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, and she has been the subject of modern plays, operas, novels and films.

timeline.title: Birth
timeline.description: Probably born in Constantinople to Acacius, bear keeper of the Green faction.

timeline.title: Meets Justinian
timeline.description: Back in the capital after years in Libya and Egypt, she meets the heir to the throne.

timeline.title: Marriage
timeline.description: After Justin I relaxes the law against actresses marrying senators, she marries Justinian.

timeline.title: Crowned augusta
timeline.description: Justinian becomes co-emperor and Theodora is crowned with him.

timeline.title: The Nika riots
timeline.description: She argues against flight as the rioters proclaim Hypatius emperor.

timeline.title: Partner in deliberation
timeline.description: Justinian's law against selling governorships makes officials swear loyalty to her as well.

timeline.title: Fall of John the Cappadocian
timeline.description: She and Antonina trap the praetorian prefect into apparent treason.

timeline.title: The Ravenna mosaic
timeline.description: The mosaic panels of Justinian and Theodora are completed in San Vitale.

timeline.title: Death
timeline.description: She dies in Constantinople and is buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.

timeline.title: Justinian at her tomb
timeline.description: The emperor lights candles at her grave during a procession through the city.
